mutation.e: Late 14th century as Middle English mutacioun, from Latin mūtātiō, both directly and via Old French mutacion.

mutilate.e: Learned borrowing from Latin mutilātus, the perfect passive participle of mutilō (“to mutilate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix))…
mutilate.x: Little old lady got mutilated late last night Werewolves of London again.

mutiny.x: In every mutiny against the discipline of the college, he was the ringleader.

mutism.e: From French mutisme, from Latin mutus (“mute”), equivalent to mute + -ism.

mutter.e: From Middle English muteren, moteren, of imitative origin. Compare Low German mustern, musseln (“to whisper”), German muttern (“to mutter.
mutter.x: You could hear the students mutter as they were served sodden spaghetti, yet again, in the cafeteria.

mutton.e: From Middle English motoun, moton, from Old French mouton (“sheep”), from Vulgar Latin moltō, from Gaulish *multon-, from Proto-Celtic *moltos (“ram, wether”).
mutton.x: Mutton, eaten with caraway seed, is eaten as an aphrodisiac among Arabs.

mutual.e: Borrowed from Middle French mutuel, from Latin mūtuus. Displaced native Old English ġemǣne.
mutual.x: They had mutual fear of each other.

muzzle.e: From earlier muzle, musle, mousle, mussel, mozell, from Middle English mosel, from Old French musel, museau, muzeau (modern French museau), from Late Latin mūsus…

mycelium.e: From New Latin mycelium; synchronically, myc- + -el- + -ium, where the infix -el- is of unknown origin, perhaps introduced from a rebracketing of epithelium.

myocardium.e: From New Latin myocardium, from Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “muscle”) + καρδίᾱ (kardíā, “heart”).

myopic.x: Corrective lenses compensate for the excessive positive diopters of the myopic eye.

myrrh.e: From Middle English mirre, from Old English myrre, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), from Semitic.
myrrh.x: A compound of eggs boiled with myrrh, pepper, and cinnamon, taken on several successive days, is recommended by Arabs for strengthening amorous vigor.

myrtle.e: From Middle English mirtille, from Old French mirtille, mirtile, from myrte, from Latin myrtillus, from myrtus + -illus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).
myrtle.x: In the Middle Ages pulverized myrtle leaves were applied to the body as a sexual stimulation.

mystic.x: Taught he not thee—the man of eld, / Whose eyes within his eyes beheld / Heaven's numerous hierarchy span / The mystic gulf from God to man?

mysticism.e: From mystic + -ism, from Old French mistique (“mysterious, full of mystery”), from Latin mysticus (“mystical, mystic, of secret rites”), from Ancient Greek μυστικός…

mythical.e: From Latin mȳthicus + -al; by surface analysis, myth + -ical.
mythical.x: He told a story about a mythical dragon.

mythological.x: In short—to be mythological in my conclusion—the quiver of Cupid hangs at the girdle of Fate together with her spindle and scissors.

mythology.e: First attested as Middle English in 1412. From Middle French mythologie, from Latin mȳthologia, from Ancient Greek μυθολογία (muthología, “legend”) μυθολογέω (muthologéō…
mythology.x: This tongue-in-cheek episode is especially fun for people who don’t take their “X-Files” mythology seriously.
